Lake sturgeon (Acipenser fulvescens) eggs are demersal and adhesive, and upon fertilisation they undergo a period of incubation linked to thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], embryos hatch after approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days], a developmental duration that aligns with the lower end of the 8-to-14-day range reported for this species. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or alevin, initially relies entirely on endogenous reserves, with the wet weight at birth measured at 0.0108 grams [Wwb = 0.0108 grams] based on the typical egg diameter of 2.74 millimetres. This modest initial mass underscores the protracted period of lecithotrophic nutrition that follows eclosion, during which the larva remains non-feeding until the yolk is largely absorbed. The timing of the trophic switch to first exogenous feeding is highly dependent on water temperature, and under controlled laboratory conditions at 13 °C, the transition is consistent with the hatching schedule described here. Such early-life metrics are crucial for parameterising population models for this long-lived species.

As the juvenile phase progresses, growth in total length becomes a defining feature of the pre-reproductive period. Field surveys indicate that puberty is attained when individuals reach a total length of 120 centimetres [Lp = 120 centimetres], a size threshold associated with the onset of gonad maturation. The time required to achieve this milestone varies between sexes when reared at a regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]; females generally require approximately 24.5 years since birth [tp = approximately 24.5 years since birth], whereas males mature somewhat earlier, at roughly 19 years since birth [tp = roughly 19 years since birth]. This sexual dimorphism in the pace of maturation is a common pattern among acipenserids and likely reflects differences in the energetic demands of vitellogenesis versus spermatogenesis. The ultimate total length recorded for the species reaches an exceptional 274 centimetres [Li = 274 centimetres], making Lake sturgeon one of the largest freshwater fish in North America. Attaining such a massive size requires many decades of sustained growth and favourable environmental conditions.

Reproductive output in Lake sturgeon is strongly tied to body size, with larger females contributing disproportionately to annual recruitment. At a total length of 135 centimetres, a gravid individual produces approximately 80 eggs per day  across the spawning period, given a four-year reproductive cycle and incubation conditions of 13 °C at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This daily rate, calculated over the entire inter-spawning interval, reflects the species' iteroparous strategy and relatively low fecundity compared to many other freshwater teleosts. For a female measuring 170.5 centimetres in total length, the corresponding reproductive output rises to about 416 eggs per day  under the same thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The marked increase in fecundity with length illustrates the strong selective advantage of continued somatic growth in this species, where each additional increment in body size yields a substantial gain in lifetime egg production. Such size-dependent reproduction is a key parameter for fisheries management.

The life span of Lake sturgeon is remarkably extended, reflecting a life-history strategy centred on delayed maturity and repeated spawning over many decades. The oldest documented individuals in protected populations reach an age of 150 years [am = 150 years] when maintained at stable thermal conditions around 13 °C [T = 13 °C], although few individuals in exploited populations survive to such advanced ages. This exceptional longevity is shared with other members of the family Acipenseridae and is linked to their slow metabolic rate, large body size, and late onset of reproductive senescence. The maximum recorded longevity places the species among the longest-lived of all freshwater fishes, rivalled only by certain paddlefish and a few deepwater ciscoes. In the wild, natural mortality from predation is highest during the egg and yolk-sac larval stages, after which survival rates increase markedly. Understanding the interplay between lifespan and reproductive output is essential for setting sustainable harvest limits.

The reproductive cycle of Lake sturgeon is characterised by long intervals between successive spawning events, a pattern that buffers the population against annual variability in environmental quality. Published accounts document that individual females spawn once every 4 to 9 years, with each spawning event yielding a single clutch of eggs per season. The frequency of these reproductive events is thus approximately 0.14 to 0.25 clutches per year, a remarkably low rate that imposes strong constraints on population recovery following overfishing. This protracted spawning periodicity is thought to reflect the high energetic cost of vitellogenesis, which requires the accumulation of substantial lipid reserves over several years of feeding. The combination of late age at maturity, long lifespan, and infrequent reproduction forms a classic K-selected life history, making the species particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbances that elevate adult mortality above natural background levels.
